common_name: Green Gem Boxwood (Dwarf Very Slow-Growing Globe Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Gem is an extremely slow-growing, dwarf Sheridan Nurseries boxwood hybrid that holds a naturally tight globe shape with minimal shearing.

directions: Green Gem is one of three cold-hardy boxwood hybrids bred by Sheridan Nurseries in Ontario by crossing English boxwood with Korean boxwood, selected as the most dwarf and slowest-growing of the group, holding a naturally neat, rounded globe form for years with only occasional light shearing. Its small, dense, rich green leaves resist the bronzing common in less hardy boxwood cultivars through cold winters, making it a dependable choice for edging, knot gardens, and small formal accents in climates too cold for English boxwood. Provide moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil and afternoon shade protection in the hottest part of zone 8-9 summers. Watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary pest of concern, and avoid heavy shearing, which is rarely needed given its inherently compact habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

common_name: Green Mound Boxwood (Cold-Hardy Irregular Mounding Boxwood)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Green Mound is a cold-hardy Sheridan Nurseries boxwood hybrid with a looser, irregularly mounded habit than its sibling selections 'Green Gem' and 'Green Velvet'.

directions: Green Mound is another of the cold-hardy Sheridan Nurseries boxwood hybrids bred from English and Korean boxwood parentage, distinguished from its sibling selections by a looser, irregularly mounded habit rather than a tight, uniform globe. Its fine-textured, small green leaves give the same year-round formal structure valued in boxwood while tolerating winters too harsh for English boxwood cultivars. The informal, undulating outline suits an unclipped foundation planting or low informal hedge where a slightly looser form than 'Green Gem' or 'Green Velvet' is wanted. Provide moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil and afternoon shade protection in the hottest part of zone 8-9 summers, and watch for boxwood leafminer, the primary Southern boxwood pest.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Dwarf Boxwood Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container-grown specimens in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained to consistently damp, acidic soil in partial to full shade; the cream leaf variegation is most pronounced with some filtered light and can green up in deep shade.

directions: Shady Lady is a variegated selection of the Gulf South native Florida anise, its glossy evergreen leaves irregularly margined in creamy white around a deep green center, brightening the same dense, shade-loving structure that makes the species such a reliable native screening shrub. Clusters of dark maroon-red, star-shaped flowers open in spring against the pale-edged foliage, and crushed or bruised leaves release the characteristic spicy anise fragrance shared by the genus. Like the species it thrives in the moist, shaded ravines and stream banks of its native range and works well as an unclipped specimen or informal screen brightening a dark corner of the shade garden. All parts are toxic if ingested, and deer generally avoid the aromatic foliage.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Swamp Hobbit Illicium (Extra-Dwarf Compact Yellow Anise)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade; Swamp Hobbit stays significantly smaller than the straight species, fitting foundation beds and small shade gardens where full-sized yellow anise would quickly outgrow the space.

directions: Swamp Hobbit is an extra-dwarf selection of small anise tree discovered for its notably compact, dense habit, staying just a few feet tall and wide compared to the towering, fast-growing straight species. It keeps the same bright lime-green, glossy, aromatic evergreen foliage and tiny, inconspicuous pale-yellow spring flowers typical of the species, valued almost entirely for its dense year-round structure rather than bloom. Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich, acidic soil in full to partial shade, where it tolerates the difficult wet, shaded conditions that challenge many broadleaf evergreens, and needs only light shaping to maintain its naturally tidy, compact form.
